title: ForkJoinPool work-stealing: own deque front, steal from back, blocking common pool is dangerous
keyPoints: Each ForkJoinPool worker thread has a double-ended queue (deque). The owner pushes and pops tasks from the front (LIFO) for cache locality.
When a worker's deque is empty, it steals tasks from the back (FIFO) of another worker's deque, taking the oldest and typically largest subtask.
Owner and thief operate at opposite ends of the deque, minimizing lock contention between them.
The common pool (ForkJoinPool.commonPool()) is shared by parallelStream(), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(), and many frameworks, sized to cores minus 1.
Blocking IO on the common pool is dangerous: blocked workers cannot steal or process tasks, causing all parallel streams and CompletableFutures to stall.
Fix: use a dedicated bounded ThreadPoolExecutor for IO-bound work, keeping the common pool reserved for CPU-bound computation.
ManagedBlocker can compensate for blocked workers by spawning temporary threads, but it is not reliable for bulk IO.

s1_definition.oneliner: ForkJoinPool uses work-stealing where each worker pops tasks from the front of its own deque (LIFO for cache locality) and idle workers steal from the back of busy workers' deques (FIFO for largest subtasks), but blocking IO on the shared common pool starves all parallel streams.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Work-stealing** – each worker thread owns a double-ended queue (deque). The worker pushes forked subtasks onto and pops tasks from the FRONT of its deque (LIFO). An idle worker steals tasks from the BACK of another worker's deque (FIFO).
- **LIFO for owner** – the most recently forked task is processed first. This subtask likely shares data with the parent, so it is hot in the CPU cache.
- **FIFO for thief** – the oldest task is stolen first. Older tasks tend to be higher up in the recursion tree and represent larger subtrees with more work, giving the thief more to do.
- **Opposite ends** – owner and thief operate at opposite ends of the deque, so they rarely contend for the same lock.
- **Common pool** – `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` is a JVM-wide singleton used by `parallelStream()`, `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync()` (no explicit executor), and many frameworks. Its parallelism is `availableProcessors() - 1`.
- **Blocking danger** – if common pool workers block on IO, they cannot steal or process tasks. Other parts of the application that rely on the common pool (any parallel stream, any default CompletableFuture) stall behind the blocked workers.
s1_definition.analogy: Each teller at National Bank of India has their own stack of forms (deque). Rajesh works from the top of his stack. When his stack is empty, he goes to Priya's desk and takes forms from the bottom of her stack. Top versus bottom means they rarely bump into each other. The common pool is like 3 shared tellers used by every department. If all 3 are stuck on long phone calls (blocking IO), no forms get processed anywhere in the bank.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Work-Stealing in ForkJoinPool
  ═════════════════════════════

  Worker-1 deque:        Worker-2 deque:
  FRONT → [D][C][B][A]   FRONT → []
          │                       │
  Worker-1 pops D (LIFO)  Worker-2 steals A from Worker-1 (FIFO)
          │                       │
  FRONT → [C][B]          FRONT → [A]

  Owner: LIFO (front) → cache locality
  Thief: FIFO (back)  → largest subtree
  Opposite ends → minimal contention
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
ForkJoinPool uses work-stealing to keep all CPU cores busy. Each worker has its own deque. The owner processes tasks from the front (LIFO for cache locality). Idle workers steal from the back of busy workers' deques (FIFO for the largest subtasks). Operating at opposite ends minimizes lock contention.

The common pool is shared by parallelStream and CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(). Blocking IO on it is dangerous because blocked workers cannot steal or process tasks, causing all parallel streams and CompletableFutures in the entire application to stall. The fix is a dedicated bounded ThreadPoolExecutor for IO work, keeping the common pool free for CPU-bound computation.

At National Bank of India, a VaR (Value at Risk) computation using parallelStream stalled for 500 milliseconds because market data HTTP calls blocked common pool workers. After segregating IO onto a dedicated pool of 30 threads, VaR computation dropped to 50 milliseconds and the common pool was always available for CPU work.

Remember one sentence: work-stealing keeps cores busy by letting idle workers take tasks from busy workers' deques, but blocking IO on the shared common pool starves the entire application.
